title: Introduction to Array
description: Understand what arrays are, how they store data, and how to access elements using index

blocks.text:
Arrays are one of the most essential data structures in all of computer science. They are the starting point the foundation on top of which countless other structures and algorithms are built.

You will run into arrays constantly, from simple iteration problems all the way to advanced techniques like two pointers, sliding window, and dynamic programming.
So… what exactly is an array?

Think of an array as a row of numbered boxes, all sitting side by side in memory. Each box holds one value, every box is the same size, and you can jump straight to any box just by knowing its number.
More precisely an array is a data structure that stores elements of the same type in a contiguous block of memory.

Imagine you need to track scores for 50 players in a game. You wouldn't write score1, score2, ..., score50 that's unmanageable.
Instead, you put them all in one array and access each score using an index: scores[0], scores[1], scores[2], and so on.
Almost every programming language starts counting from zero, so the very first element lives at index 0.
Reading any element is extremely fast because every element sits right next to the previous one in memory. The CPU can calculate the exact memory address of any index using a single formula:
Memory address formula:
address of arr[i] = base_address + (i × size_of_one_element)
This is why reading any element whether it's at index 0 or index 999,999 always takes constant time: O(1).
But arrays do have a limitation.

In lower-level languages like C and C++, an array's size is locked in at the moment you create it. Declare space for 50 elements, and that's all you ever get. Need a 51st? You have to create a brand new, bigger array and copy every element across that costs O(n) time.
Most modern languages sidestep the fixed-size problem by offering a smarter version:
These are called dynamic arrays. They grow on their own as you add more elements.
But how does that actually work under the hood?
A dynamic array secretly allocates more slots than it currently needs. So if you've added 4 elements, it might have already reserved space for 8:

Now that you know how arrays are laid out in memory, let's look at the operations you'll use constantly and how efficient each one actually is.
1. Accessing by Index
Because every element's address can be calculated instantly, reading a value at any index is a single step no matter how large the array is.

codes.python:
scores = [95, 82, 74, 60, 88]

# Read the element at index 3
index = 3
value = scores[index]

print(f"Score at index {index} = {value}")

blocks.text: Output
This is always O(1) grab ten elements or ten million, the time doesn't change.
2. Traversal
Traversal means stepping through every element in order — used for things like totalling values, printing all items, or finding a specific one.

codes.python:
temperatures = [31, 28, 35, 29, 33]

# Visit every element once and sum it
total = sum(temperatures)

average = total / len(temperatures)

print(f"Total: {total}, Average: {average:.1f}")

blocks.text: Output
Each element is visited exactly once, so traversal takes O(n) time it scales with the size of the array.
3. Insertion
Where you insert determines how fast the operation is.
Appending to the end is cheap you just drop the new value into the next available slot. That's O(1).
Inserting at the beginning or middle is expensive. Every element to the right of the insertion point has to shift one position forward to make room. In the worst case, that's O(n) shifts.
Even if Python or Java handles that shifting invisibly for you, the cost is still there.
3.1 Insert at the Beginning

codes.python:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 40]

arr.insert(0, 5)  # insert at beginning

for x in arr:
    print(x, end=" ")

4. Deletion
Deletion follows the same pattern as insertion.
Removing the last element is instant just shrink the size by one. That's O(1).
Removing from the start or middle means every element after the gap has to slide one position left to close it. That's O(n).
Remove index 0 from an array of 5,000 elements and 4,999 elements have to move. That cost adds up.
4.1 Delete from Beginning

codes.python:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

arr.pop(0)  # delete first element

for x in arr:
    print(x, end=" ")

blocks.text: Output
4.2 Delete from End

codes.python:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

arr.pop()  # delete last element

for x in arr:
    print(x, end=" ")

blocks.text: Output
4.3 Delete from Middle

codes.python:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

del arr[2]  # delete element at index 2

for x in arr:
    print(x, end=" ")

blocks.text: Output
5. Search
How fast you can find something depends entirely on whether the array is sorted.
In an unsorted array, there's no shortcut you check each element one by one until you find a match. Worst case: O(n).
In a sorted array, you can use Binary Search. It repeatedly cuts the remaining search range in half, so it only needs O(log n) steps to find anything.
5.1 Linear Search (Unsorted Array) O(n)
If the array is not sorted, we check each element one by one.

blocks.text: 2. Sliding Window
Used when a problem asks you to look at a contiguous subarray or substring.
Instead of recalculating from scratch every time the window moves, you slide it one step adding the new right element and dropping the old left element.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785249441846-703537294.png
blocks.alt: Sliding window of size 3 summing to 11

blocks.text: window of size 3 → sum = 11
slide right → drop 3, add 8 → sum = 16
slide right → drop 6, add 5 → sum = 15
Done cleverly, sliding window reduces a brute-force O(n²) down to O(n).
This technique is extremely useful for problems like:

items: Maximum or minimum sum of a fixed-size subarray
Longest subarray satisfying a given condition

blocks.text: 3. Prefix Sum
Prefix sums let you answer "what is the sum from index L to index R?" in O(1) even though the original calculation would normally take O(n).
You precompute a running total array first, then answer any range query using:
sum(L → R) = prefix[R] − prefix[L − 1]
Input array:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785249446279-66720077.png
Prefix sum array:
Want the sum from index 1 to 4? That's
prefix[4] − prefix[0] = 24 - 3 = 21.
One subtraction instead of four additions.
This becomes critical when you have hundreds of range queries on the same array without prefix sums each query costs O(n), with them each costs O(1).
4. Dynamic Programming (DP)
Arrays are the backbone of most dynamic programming solutions.
The idea: instead of solving the same sub-problem over and over again through recursion, you store each result in an array the moment you compute it. Future steps just look it up.
The dp array here is doing all the heavy lifting storing answers to sub-problems so we never repeat work.
